newsitem.title: USA: Collectors cool to Einstein letters to first wife.
newsitem.headline: Collectors cool to Einstein letters to first wife.

text.p: The market value of Albert Einstein's scientific writings rose on Monday, but his status as a correspondence celebrity crashed at a public auction held at Christie's.
Jeremy Norman, a book dealer from California, paid $398,500 for an Einstein manuscript that documented his search for empirical proof of his theory of relativity.

But a celebrated archive of 400 intimate family letters available for the first time at auction failed to bring in the minimum reserve bid settled on by Einstein's estate and was knocked down in 115 lots.

The most talked-about of the lots, the 43 "love letters" written to his first wife, Mileva Maric, were bought by an unidentified telephone bidder for $442,500, less than the minimum bid of $500,000 estimated by the auction house.
"We're very happy to have sold it," Christie's spokesman Stephen Massey said of the lot.
The manuscript dealing with relativity exceeded its estimated top price of $350,000.
"I was very satisfied with the first sale," Massey said. "The second was spotty."
Massey explained why he thought a manuscript of mathematical calculations had brought more than expected while the controversial love/hate letters were soft.
"I think Einstein will be known as a scientist," he said. "The media was more interested in portraying him as a family man, but in the end, he'll be viewed as a scientist, not as a family man."
Although some experts said the letters shed little light on the unhappiness of Einstein's first marriage, the general public may be surprised at his old-fashioned male chauvinism.

Einstein met Maric when he was 17 and they were both at the Zurich Polytechnic Institute in 1896, and he fell in love with the Serbian woman four years his senior. In his first letters to her, he calls her "kitten" and says, "Without the thought of you, I would no longer want to live among this sorry herd of humans."

By 1901 he and Maric had had a daughter out of wedlock. The little girl's fate is not known, but it is believed Maric gave her up for adoption and Einstein never saw her, although in the 1930s he employed private detectives to find her.

The couple were married in 1903, but by 1913 their union, which produced two sons, was on the rocks. Einstein wrote his cousin, Elsa, who later became his second wife, that he treated Maric "like an employee whom I cannot fire."
By 1914 Einstein was setting down rules for Maric if she expected to stay with him.
